title: Can the paper protractor measure these two angles?
description: Two angles at the vertex H are measured with a protractor. Then each reading is checked against the creases of the paper protractor made by folding, to see whether the paper protractor can be used.
teaching_notes: One idea: a paper protractor made by folding can measure only the angles that lie exactly on its creases. Watch for students who round a reading to the nearest crease and call it the measure.

source: Figure it Out (after Angle Bisector), Q3
video_script.why: The child measures two angles by the three checks of the solved example, and sees why the paper protractor of the book is not enough for them.
video_script.substitution: The two angles IHJ of the book's question, one in each drawing.
video_script.anchor: the two drawings of the book, each with the angle IHJ at the vertex H, and the paper protractor with its creases
video_script.payoff_line: The angles measure forty two and one hundred and sixteen degrees

final_answer.value: 42°, 116°; the paper protractor cannot be used here
final_answer.spoken: the paper protractor cannot work here

maths_rules: the first angle IHJ reads 42 degrees
the second angle IHJ reads 116 degrees
the paper protractor is made by folding a straight angle of 180 degrees into eight equal parts, so each part is 180 / 8 = 22.5 degrees
the creases lie at 22.5, 45, 67.5, 90, 112.5, 135 and 157.5 degrees
42 lies between the creases 22.5 and 45, and 116 lies between the creases 112.5 and 135, so neither lies on a crease
video_script.design: The two drawings stay on the board. A protractor measures each angle, and then the creases of the paper protractor are laid beside the readings; the readings are held back until the answer line.
